Psalm 22

(1) Includes multiple cry outs to God regarding the reality of the circumstances
(2) Includes multiple mentions of God’s goodness, and a remembrance of what he’s done. 
(3) Includes the consequences of God’s intervention or lack thereof. “I will praise you, for your name’s 
      sake, can the dead praise you? etc.”
(4) Cry out for help, comfort, deliverance, etc. 

No particular order here except acknowledging what’s real first. 

(1) psalms and other places point show us what grieving looks like. Job, Lazarus, Saul’s sons
(2) Acknowledging the reality of what’s happened. Take time to feel what is real. 
(3) Grief provokes either to pride/shame or to humility
(4) Express our grief, fear, anger, etc to God directly. Prayer, worship, other artistic expression, silence
(5) Confess our struggles to others who are trustworthy also focus on new experiences

Purpose in pain: 
(1) What's the reward for grieving well?
(2) What are God's promises to those who grieve well?
(3) Joseph and his brothers
(4) Paul's thorn in the flesh
(5) Those who leave behind wordly goods, family, etc. for Christ. 
(6) Using the testimony of God's help to serve him

Here is booklet one, this one is written more to the general Church audience as an introduction to grieving in a Godly way. It's not meant to be a specific guide for group leaders or staff members, but accesible to anyone who picks it up:

	   		GOOD GRIEF: Finding God’s Best During Life’s Worst

Jesus says, “In this world you will have trouble” (John 16:33). Faith in God doesn’t give us a life free of pain, failure, or disappointment. At some point, all of us will experience something difficult, with some of us experiencing far more than others. 

There are many kinds of these troubles. They range from the pressure of higher academics and competitive career positions, to the day to day grind in various things, to relational strife, to loosing loved ones, or facing threats to our own safety, even to our very lives. 

Whatever the trouble is, it will produce some kind of grief in our life. Without understanding what grief is, we can’t grieve well, and we miss out on many of the things God wants us to gain from our struggles. Wisdom, peace, worship, purpose, deliverance, joy, spiritual maturity, and many other good things wait for those who are willing to grieve. A shallow, bitter, disconnected, and seemingly senseless life waits for those who are not. 

What Is Grief:

Grief can’t be defined by a single word. It’s more like a family of words describing different emotions and conditions that trouble the soul. If we look at Isiah 53:3 we can see how two of these words help us understand the rest. 

“He was despised and rejected by men, a man of sorrows and acquainted with grief;
and as one from whom men hide their faces he was despised, and we esteemed him not.” 

The Hebrew word for sorrows in this verse, makʾōv, means emotional anguish, which is what we normally mean when we say grief in English. But a different Hebrew word is translated into the English word grief here, and that’s the word ḥōlî, which refers more to the conditions that produce emotional anguish, than the anguish itself. 

When you put these words together, you get a more complete picture. Moving forward, when I say grief, I’m referring to that complete picture. When I say grieving, I’m referring to the process of dealing with both. 

When Grief is Out of Place

Nobody wants to grieve. The idea of suffering the circumstances that cause grief and having to sort through the emotional fallout just isn’t attractive. Because of this, most of the time people don’t learn how to grieve unless they have to. 

Most of the American Church today hasn’t been forced to grieve anywhere near as much as the Church in other areas of the world and at other times. That safety and prosperity has come at a cost though, which is we haven’t learned how to put grief or grieving in their place. In our lack of perspective, we often place these things in the wrong spot in our lives. 

Lost In Grief

For some, in spite how unpleasant grieving can be, their perspective ends up revolving around their pain. Whether they have gone through much or little, it takes center stage of their life and they can’t seem to escape its hold on them. Their preoccupation with grief ends up creating problems that don’t have to exist, and the tools God created to process through pain become a source of pain instead.

Our grief, no matter how severe or prolonged, was never meant to take center stage in our lives. When it does, it suffocates our faith, filling our field of view in a way that ends up occupying the space that God alone is supposed to have in our hearts and minds. It prevents us from seeing God’s goodness, enjoying his blessings, recognizing our responsibilities, and seeing ourselves as God’s beloved.

When the pain is all a person can feel, it’s only natural for this to happen and despair becomes the unfortunate, but understandable result. Understandable as it is though, it still remains unjustified because we serve a supernatural God who who’s existence goes beyond what we can feel. 

He’s bigger than the problem, and while their expectations have no doubt been shaped by their experiences, those experiences can lead people to wrong conclusions. God doesn’t want people to stay stuck in those wrong conclusions that keep them in a place of misery. Even if deliverance is slow, or only partial in this life, Jesus did not die for them and rise from the dead, just so that grief could become their God instead of him.

Lost In Denial 

Others live in denial. They bury themselves in work, in school, relationships, etc. So long as they just keep distracted, they don’t even see the need to sort through the damage life has done to them. Often, because they are so distracted, they don’t even see the damage to begin with. 

These people often report much higher levels of satisfaction in life, but under careful examination, that satisfaction proves to be more of a feeling than a fact. A life where someone can’t or won’t grieve is a life that is void of the blessings that are reserved only for those who’ve known heartbreak, and what it means to mourn.

Jesus points to this in Matt: 5: 3-4 “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted”.

When someone doesn’t receive God’s comfort in their own grief, they can’t comfort others properly as they grieve (2 Corinthians 2:4). This absence is a serious issue, because it robs a person of maturity in their relationships with God and others. Jesus understood this and took the idea of going to the father with his needs and grief seriously. 

If Jesus acted like his grief didn’t exist, if he didn’t bother going to the Father with it, he just wouldn’t be the Jesus we see in the Bible, he’d be someone else. He wouldn’t be able to follow his own teaching and mourn with those who mourned. He wouldn’t be able to comforted others who were afflicted, or do many other things if he never shared his heart with the Father. 

If we act like our grief doesn’t exist, or is no big deal, if we won’t go to the Father, then how can we be like Jesus? Truthfully, we can’t. Choosing to avoid our grief is the same as choosing to avoid him.

					Putting Grief in Its Place

With both extremes common, it’s important to know where grief actually belongs in our life. If it’s not to be ignored, and not to be obsessed over, what should be done with grief and grieving?

The answer isn’t intuitive, but it is life changing. Instead of these extremes, we should look at grief and grieving in a similar way to worship, miracles and providence.

That’s right, I compared the worst things that can happen to a person on this earth and the ordeal of being forced to sort through those things to miracles, worship, and God providing through the day to day mundane things. But why?

All of these things are signs. Grief points to the insufficiency of the world in providing for our needs and enjoyment. Miracles and providence start where grief leaves off, and then point to God’s sufficiency in ways the world can’t compete with. Worship, in particular lamentation, shows us how to point our grief to God’s face, instead of hiding it or taking it to others behind his back (figuratively). 

Grief as a Sign

In John 1: 9-7, we see a great example of this:

“As he passed by, he saw a man blind from birth. And his disciples asked him, “Rabbi, who sinned, this man, or his parents, that he was born blind?” Jesus answered, “It was not that this man sinned, or his parents, but that the works of God might be displayed in him”.

The gravity of the blind man’s grief naturally provoked the question of why things happened they way they did. It’s normal and healthy to want to understand why bad things happened. But while it is normal, it isn’t healthy for the disciples to make the presumptions about this man or his parents in the way they did. 

This is where we begin to find out that this man’s grief wasn’t just about him. The way they looked at his pain became a window into the condition of their hearts and minds. This window wouldn’t have opened unless they noticed something significantly out of place and that is where we start to see some purpose in this man’s pain.

To be clear, the reason why there is grief in our lives, the reason why there has to be grief in our lives is because it exposes the condition of our hearts in ways that nothing else can. Nothing else can point to our guilt, our shame, our ignorance, or any need we have more than the suffering that comes from sin and living in a broken world. 

Without grief, we are lost in darkness even more so than the man born blind. We become incapable of recognizing Jesus as the light, because we don’t even have a reference point to compare what is light vs. what is dark. 

Grief provides essential contrast, effectively setting the stage for God to display who he is and show us the difference between himself and all other gods, ideas, and ways of living. A person who’s never grieved will never truly know the difference between what’s hot and cold, right and wrong, or even what’s dead or alive spiritually speaking. That is grief’s primary job, to let us know what is dead. 

Miracles as a Sign

If grief is there to to show us what is dead, what is there to show us what is alive? 

In the same passage about the man born blind, we see Jesus heal him. He conquers this man’s grief and corrects those who would condemn him. All while liberating someone imprisoned by the work of the evil one and not by his own doing.

While this event is amazing, it’s not actually the point of the story. Just as the man’s grief revealed the condition of the disciples’ hearts, Jesus’s response to the man’s grief reveals the condition of God’s heart. It shows that it’s not his intention to waste our pain, but rather to give us purpose in the midst of it. 

Yet even that purpose is only part of the point. So then what is it? 

The point of miracles is to reveal God’s identity and authority as seen in the way he responds to our pain. God is far more than just his compassion. The miracles that point to his compassion also point to his holiness, his authority, his wisdom, and every other aspect of his nature. It’s not just that he cares, but that  he actually has the power to do something about it, even when naturally nothing can be done. 

If miracles are so powerful, and they are such a powerful way to pointing to who God, does this mean that God’s answer to our grief must be found in miracles?

The answer is no. For most of Church history since the Apostles death, miracles haven’t been common at all. If miracles alone were how God responds to grief, there would be few people who ever knew God’s heart indeed. 

Now some have made the claim that miracles entirely stopped after the early Church, but we have a long history of reports from highly influential figures such as Augustine, Gregory the Great, and Thomas Becket that contradict those claims. My own experiences, and what I read from scripture regarding what to expect from God also contradict those claims. So saying that miracles aren’t a thing anymore simply goes too far for me.

Still, if they aren’t happening as much as before, what does God do to respond to our grief that can be easily found compared to searching for the supernatural? What’s available to everyone who believes, and not just those who’ve personally experienced a miracle. 

Providence as a Sign

To find the answer, we have to start looking for what God does with normal things. There’s a term that covers this idea called “providence”. This means that God works through ordinary things, yet is not limited by them and can do what he wants regardless of how he chooses to do it. 

Just as with miracles, providence shows us God’s response to our grief and points to who he is. Unlike miracles, providence shows us that his answer doesn’t have to be showy or sensational to be powerful. In fact, it can be some of the most common things we can think of.  

In Hosea 11, we see God describing his own grief towards Israel. Part of that description involves how he used human relationships in his efforts to raise the nation, just as a parent would use tender means to raise their own child. He then expresses grief in response to how that kindness has been ignored. In verse 4 we see:

I led them with cords of human kindness, with ties of love. To them I was like one who lifts
a little child to the cheek, and I bent down to feed them. 

The phrase cords of human kindness here is really important. The Hebrew word for cords is kheh-’bel and the other is adām. Not the English name Adam, but the Hebrew word for human. The picture here is like someone leading a creature on a leash, but in this case, God’s leash is human love and Israel is far more than just a pet or prized animal.

The kindness God is referring to here shows up in every act of love between husband and wife, parents and children, and the kindness between neighbors. In every type of loving personal interaction, God is present. These times of blessing were not without grief, yet God’s presence in these interactions shows he was at work to take care of his people not just by working for them, but also through them.

We can see God at work this way when he guides Abraham’s servant in finding a wife for Isaac after his mother’s death (Genesis 24). We can see him at work in the way Boaz took interest in protecting Ruth (Ruth 2:8-9), and how Ruth took interest in taking care of her mother in-law (Ruth 2: 11-12). We can see this in how the people of Israel took part in the both diligent and dangerous work of repairing Jerusalem’s walls (Nehemiah 4:13-21), and in many other situations.

In all these things, it’s very clear that God isn’t limited to supernatural actions to deliver and sustain his people, even under the most stressful of times. He can use anything he chooses to lead his people to himself and teach them to rely on his kindness. Just like with miracles, God uses that trust to point us away from grief and to himself, preventing us from getting stuck on grief or lost in denial.

All the Signs Point To…

When grief is in its proper place, something that naturally points to death ends up pointing to life instead. Grief points to the spiritual bankruptcy in our lives, the hardships of this world and death itself. Miracles and providence show Gods response to death and everything that leads to it. Our God is the author of life, and ultimately, grief is supposed to point to him.

				Grieving Well: God’s Path to Blessing

At this point, I want to shift attention away from God’s general providence, and focus on something a little bit more specific. There’s perhaps one thing more than any other that allows us to experience God’s providence in the midst of our grief, and that’s a combination of mourning and lamentation. Ideas which are both common in the Bible, but in modern terms, we usually call grieving.

Just for clarity, grieving includes both the inner experience of grief and its outer, often verbal expression. The heaviness and brokenness of our hearts, the bitterness, the temptations to despair, etc. are all included. Prayers, songs, and other forms of expression, many of which are artistic, are also included. 

Sadly, much of the American Church doesn’t want to grieve or doesn’t know how. We’re mostly focused on a shallow version of praise that glosses over our pain and outwardly shows something that looks like faith, but inwardly amounts to little more than denial. We think the answer is to just pray, just believe, just keep reading scripture so we can focus on God’s goodness and somehow the rest will fall into place. It is complete nonsense!

On the other extreme, a smaller portion of the Church outwardly praises God, but inwardly gives their grief God-like status in their heart. They sing the songs and say the things out of habit, but can’t get past the sin they think they can’t be cleansed of, the trauma suffered from someone else’s hands, or the hardship of life in general.

But when the hype fades and the suffering remains, the only things left from these approaches to pain are hypocrisy, doubt, disbelief, cynicism, and other poisons to the soul. Praise that doesn’t acknowledge the reality, including the limits of our pain isn’t praise at all. It’s a slap in the face to the God who keeps a record of our tears (Psalm 56:8), is the source of all comfort (2 Cor 1:3-4), and is publicly vulnerable in how he faces his own pain. (Hosea 11, Mark 15:34, Luke 22: 43-44). 

Well what about praise that does acknowledge the pain, what do we get from that? The answer is we get the first step to blessings that aren’t available to us under any other conditions. When we look at Jesus say “blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven”, and “blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted”, we get a preview of this. 

This means only if we’re willing to experience a broken heart in God’s presence, will we be able to take part in his kingdom. If we’re willing to grieve well, we’re willing to have connection with the Father, who the Bible describes as the “God of all comfort”. The same can be said for connection with his people. As we sacrifice our grief to God through honest expression, we let go of the pride, the fear, the shame etc. that would bar us from his presence and shut the doors of heaven. 

As we grieve, we given a promise in Psalm 34:18: 

“The Lord is near to the broken hearted and rescues those with a crushed spirit.” 

It’s only under these conditions where God’s providence in giving comfort to his people shines the most. Paul speaks of this in 2nd Corinthians 1: 3-10. 

To Paraphrase, he says that God comforts us in all our afflictions, that the Father is the God of all comfort, and that we can comfort others with the comfort we get from God. He then go so far as to say that his trials had grieved him so much that he had even despaired of life at one point, so he’s not talking about comfort for trivial things here. 

That comfort changes us. As we work through the pain, it gives us an experiential knowledge of God’s love, the kind of knowledge that changes our hearts in a way that allows us to rejoice even while we are grieving (Rom 5:1-5). 

It’s only out of the joy we experience in our grief, that we can comfort others. I’m not talking about feeling happy, or painting on a fake smile, but the conviction of God’s goodness and the enjoyment of his love that doesn’t depend on circumstances. As we learn this joy, we gain insight, wisdom, compassion, patience, etc. in ways that just aren’t available to those who don’t know God’s comfort.  

Once we have these things, the act of serving God by sharing what he’s given us allows us to experience connection with God in a way that Jesus describes as food (John 4: 32-34). This is a form of nourishment for our souls and something that nurtures contentment in our lives. 

We can see the effect this has on Paul as time goes on. In spite of the many sufferings he speaks of, he says this in Philippians 4:12-13

 “I know how to be brought low, and I know how to abound. In any and every circumstance I have learned the secret of facing plenty and hunger, abundance and need. I can do all things through Christ who strengthens me.”

We see again in 2nd Corinthians 12: 7-10

“So to keep me from becoming conceited because of the surpassing greatness of the revelations, a thorn was given to me in the flesh, a messenger of Satan to harass me, to keep me from becoming conceited. Three times I pleaded with the Lord about this, that it should leave me. But he said to me, “My grace is sufficient for you, my power is made perfect in weakness.” Therefore I will boast all the more gladly of my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may rest upon me.”

Paul’s contentment, even his boasting, rested on receiving God’s comfort and strength in response to his own pain and weakness. Paul doesn’t talk about a life free of trials because he’s faithful (2nd Corinthians 11: 23-30), he points out the opposite. Both his trials and his deliverance are directly connected to his faith. They represent an essential part of part of the process that God uses to mature him. 

When Paul tells us to imitate him as he imitates Jesus(1 Cor 11:1), he wants us to follow the example of faithful reliance on the Father that they both set for us. Only when we do this, can we learn to boast in God’s strength the way Paul boasted, and how to be content in all circumstances because we can do all things through Christ who strengthens us. 

Once we’ve learned that contentment, it’s easier to understand Paul cin acts 20:35.

“In all things I have shown you that by working hard in this way we must help the weak and remember the words of the Lord Jesus, how he himself said, ‘It is more blessed to give than to receive”

To sum up the path to blessing; you can’t give what you don’t have, and you won’t have God’s comfort if you’re unwilling to grieve with God help. If you want to understand how it’s more blessed to give to others then receive from them, grieve with God’s help first. Then you will know his joy in blessing you. Then you can know the joy of blessing others. 

						How To Grieve

So now that we know why we should grieve, let’s look at how to grieve. 

Fighting Denial: Truthfulness and transparency.

The hardest part of grieving is just getting started. In modern terms, grief is often divided up into stages, with denial being the first barrier we must overcome. There’s a multitude of sins, fears, and other reasons that make it harder to make the choice to deal with the real world. But once we can take an honest look at things, all the distractions and all the overwhelming moments put together can’t compare to the power of admitting the truth.

We see an example of this 2nd Samuel 11 and 12 with the story of David’s adultery with Bathsheba, his 
murder of Uriah her husband and Nathan the prophet confronting him some time after. To summarize, David committed several evil acts all stung together to create one of the most disgraceful and treacherous series of events in Israel’s history. 

David shows several cases of denial here, each one leading to a more serious crime than the last. First, he ignores his responsibility to lead his nation in war. Then, while out of harms way in his palace, he sends for Bathsheba after choosing to stare at her from a rooftop as she is Bathing. He then commits adultery with her, a crime punishable by death under mosaic law (Lev. 20:10). 

After he finds out she is pregnant, he tries to be clever and bring Uriah back to the front line and get him to lay with his wife, an act that soldiers typically would not do during times of war (Deut. 23:10, 1 Samuel 21: 5-6). When this fails, he then sends a letter to Uriah’s commanding officer to arrange for his death by betraying him in battle (2nd Samuel 11:14-17).

Finishing the story, for a while it seems that David has gotten away with his treachery, until God sends Nathan the prophet to confront him. In a display of wit and courage, Nathan exposes David’s sin clear as day and finally David relents. David failed his duties as King and father. Consequently, his family in some ways is left unprotected against the evils of sickness, perversion, rebellion and even death. But his own life is spared as a result of his confession. 

We don’t have to harden our hearts the way he did for so long. We don’t need to bring on ourselves discipline or judgment. We don’t need to drag those we are responsible for taking care of down with us. What we need to do is to start where David finished. If God was merciful to David by sparing at least his life, he can be merciful to us as well. 
 
Expressing Grief:

Once we can be honest with ourselves, we need to be honest with God also. That means going through a process of sorting out everything that’s connected to the truth we’ve been forced to confront. It involves taking an honest look at every corner of our heart, no matter how uncomfortable our anger, sorrow, confusion, etc. might be.

But we’re not meant to do this by ourselves, nor are we meant to do this without the truths we need to protect us in the process. If we just rush in, we’ll find out the hard way there’s a reason why people are so quick to deny things. The threat is real. It’s severe enough to be responsible for many thousands of deaths of despair every year in this country alone, most of which involve people who aren’t getting help, or aren’t getting enough of it. 

So what does a responsible expression of grief look like? First and foremost, it looks like inviting God into our hearts, into the moment, and taking the time to express things to him directly and in full. It also looks like keeping in mind everything we’ve learned about the character and goodness of God, even if we don’t feel it at the moment, or perhaps have never really felt much of it at all. Finally, it looks like inviting those you know have compassion and wisdom into the process to grieve with you.

Invitation:

When we think of an invitation, we often think of a card or some other polite greeting. But inviting God into our grief isn’t always polite. As much as it’s a good thing to approach God in a measured, considerate way, the reality is that the worst of our grief can, and in some cases should lead us to approach our Father in heaven more like a distressed child than a calm, collected adult. 

We can see one example of this in Jeremiah 20:7-8:

“O Lord, you have deceived me, and I was deceived; you are stronger than I, and you have prevailed.
I have become a laughingstock all the day; everyone mocks me. For whenever I speak, I cry out, I shout, “Violence and destruction!” For the word of the Lord has become for me a reproach and derision all day long.”

We know that God can’t lie (Hebrews 6:18), yet Jeremiah opens his lament with what appears to be a baseless accusation. But behind this is something more profound. In the next verse Jeremiah talks about how he can’t stop speaking God’s word, in spite of all the grief it’s causing him as if it is an unbearable burden. It’s safe to say he feels as if he’s served God in vain, a theme that comes up during Job’s suffering as well (Job 34:9).

Jeremiah goes even further in chapter 20 verses 14-18, cursing the day he was born and wishing he’d never seen the light of day! Most of us would dismiss all of this as complaining and not see the value in it, but God knows our shortsightedness and includes things like this in scripture for a reason. We see the same depth of grief expressed elsewhere, such as psalm 88, psalm 22 and many other places. 

This is what it looks like to invite God into the fullness of our pain. Yes, we should be respectful. Yes, it’s important to not just complain or grumble. But any portion of our hearts we hide from him is the same portion we reserve for our pride and our shame. Job, David, Jeremiah and Jesus himself all shared the depth of their grief with the Father like this, we should do the same. 

Remembrance:

The greatest difference between complaining and lamenting isn’t the depth of what’s expressed, it’s the purpose of the expression. We need to know why we’re saying what we’re saying. If we’re doing nothing but venting our spirit, God’s word calls that foolish (Prov 29:11). We need to do something else as well, which is remember who it is we’re speaking too. 
In the same chapter as before, Jeremiah also says this:

“But the Lord is with me as a dread warrior; therefore my persecutors will stumble; they will not overcome me. They will be greatly shamed, for they will not succeed. Their eternal dishonor will never be forgotten.”

With that statement and others, he mixes grief with praise and doesn’t loose sight of the fact that there is a point to expressing his grief, knowing God does care about it, and that he can do something about it also. 

In psalm 88, we see an even greater emphasis on grief, yet there is still an acknowledgment of God’s goodness at the beginning. The multiple mentions in that psalm of crying out imply the author knows there’s a God who is listening and willing to provide comfort, even if he seems far off. 

Our lamentation needs to be done in this context or it will turn into complaining, bitterness, turning our backs on God passively, or even openly cursing him. If our “lamentation” turns into nothing but a self-pity party, we can eventually convince ourselves that we’re entirely innocent, that God owes us everything and we owe him nothing. 

Inviting others:

Our grief isn’t meant to be shared with God alone. We are told to weep with those who weep (Rom 12:5), carry each other’s burdens (Gal 6:2), and that if one of us suffers, all suffer together(1 cor 12:26). This means that bringing other people into the grieving process isn’t something we do if we feel like it, it’s a holy way of life.

But if the Father is the God of all comfort, then why do other people need to be involved? The answer is that God is a relational God, who created us in his image and desires for us to not merely be in relationship with him, but also with each other. He provides comfort in our suffering not merely for our own sake, but for the sake of others, as well as his own glory. 

If we look again at 2nd Corinthians 1: 6-7, we see the relational side of things play out in a little more detail:

“If we are afflicted, it is for your comfort and salvation; and if we are comforted, it is for your comfort, which you experience when you patiently endure the same sufferings that we suffer.  Our hope for you is unshaken, for we know that as you share in our sufferings, you will also share in our comfort.”

We see God at work in this verse the same way as we saw in Hosea, where the actions of God’s people are the means he chooses to raise a nation, just as a parent would raise their own child. With this in mind, we invite others into our grieving and we grieve with others because it’s evidence of God at work, helping us to work out our relationship with him, knowing that he’s behind our efforts (Phil 2:12-13). 

The benefits of grieving together are clear in scripture. We safer and better provided for (Prov. 4:9-12). We position ourselves for healing (James 5:6). We protect our hearts from hardening (Hebrews 3:12-13). But perhaps most poignant, we fulfill the law of Christ (Gal. 6:2). God’s word is very clear on this, we are not meant to suffer on our own. 

						Moving Forward

I’ll talk about the final stage of grief here, accepting what’s happened in full and finding God’s purpose in the pain.

Here is the second booklet. This one is written specifically for group leaders, staff members, or other volunteers who are working directly under the supervison of Church leadership as part of official Church ministry. This one is less about what grief is and how to deal with it in general, but more specifically on how to mentor someone who is gouing through severe difficulties. It's mostly finished, although I would like to structure it in a way that includes the addition at the end into the main document in a more seamless way. 

I'd like to put an introduction to both of them explaining who I am, my own trauma backround and how I've recovered over the years. Obviously I'm not going into a lot of sensitive details in the introduction, but I want readers to know I'm speaking from a position of credible first-hand experience and not just theory. 

Mentoring the Most Vulnerable Among Us
Jesus says, “In this world you will have trouble” (John 16:33). Faith in God doesn’t give us a life free of pain, failure, or disappointment. At some point, all of us will experience something difficult, with some of us experiencing far more than others. 

Our hope with this ministry is to reach out to those who are most hurting. Our aim is to bring the compassion and wisdom of Jesus into their life to help them overcome their trials and better experience his love. 
This guide is meant to equip you in how you approach the broken. We want to help you avoid common pitfalls and prepare you to walk through these trials with your mentee. The preparation you do ahead of time is essential. So much so, you are more likely to harm than help someone without it
Our character is what shows our preparation. It is from character that we minister to others. It is by character we set an example. While this guide isn’t comprehensive, it will give you a brief view of what your character should be before taking on this responsibility.   
Part 1: Humility and Patience
Verses to consider
    • Job 2: 11-13 (Don’t rush to conclusions)
    • 1 Thess. 5:13 (Showing patience before acting)
    • Prov. 18:13 / 19:2 (The folly of speaking in ignorance or hastily)

(Job 2: 11-13) Job’s friends rightfully get a lot of criticism in the way they treat their friend, but we can still learn from the few things they did well. Let’s look at some of those things which were helpful.
    • They acknowledged how bad the situation was. 
    • They mourned with him. 
    • They withheld their judgment and didn’t rush to conclusions.
 At first, Job’s friends show humility and patience. By not passing judgment, rushing to conclusions, or denying the situation, they showed the kind of heart posture needed for this kind of ministry (if only they stayed that way!). 

If we do the opposite, we think we’re helping them, but the truth is we have some sort of wrong motive involved. Love is patient, love is not proud,  so if you don’t have the patience and humility to learn what’s actually going on, you’re not acting out of love. Job’s friends didn’t do well overall, so please learn from their few successes and act out of love.
(1 Thess. 5:13) Moving to first Thessalonians, we see that patience is more than a lesson we can learn from Job’s friends, it’s commanded for everyone. Many people approach these situations with a “drive by Jesus” attitude, thinking that a quick phrase or reminder of something encouraging will make the difference. 
Others just rush into trying to help in practical ways without any real effort to understand the nature of the needs they are trying to meet. Yet we’re told specifically to “have patience with them all”. What does having patience look like?
    •  Listening before we speak.
    •  Asking questions to understand the situation before giving answers.
    •  Not acting in haste or without wisdom.
(Prov. 18:13 / 19:2) What happens if we ignore the command to be patient in first Thessalonians? There are many issues, but the most severe of them is we act out of pride. The proverbs denounce pride-driven impatience as shameful and foolish. These are not accusations to take lightly, so it’s critical that we learn to recognize this problem before it fully sets in.

How can we recognize when our pride is preventing us from being patient? Look for the issues listed below. You will need to have good self-awareness to do this, but also be willing to hear about it from others who can see what you can’t.
    • Don’t be unteachable, refusing to change course even with evidence against you.
    • Don’t be agenda driven, you will create emotional and spiritual boundary issues. 
    • Don’t be an accuser, repeating the mistakes Job’s friends are best known for.
Putting all this together: 

If we show patience, we show humility. Humility helps us to follow the wisdom in the proverbs and to not repeat the mistakes of Job’s friends. As we do this, we minimize the mistakes we make as we try to figure out how to best help those in our care. 
I want to end this section with a strong warning. We need humility to protect the mentee from paying the price for our pride. It’s bad enough if they run into us unprepared, even if we are willing to learn from our mistakes, because they are the ones paying the cost of our tuition. 
But when we’re not prepared and still proud, we force them to pay our tuition in vain. Our stubbornness leads us to place a heavy burden them. This burden is opposite of God’s heart and can threaten to crush someone’s soul (Matt: 12:20). 

If we do this, we become the stumbling block Mentioned in Matt 18:6. Jesus doesn’t mince words here, your mentee is better without you anywhere near their struggles, or perhaps anywhere near them at all depending how bad it is. Don’t take this lightly. 
 Part 2: Transparency
Verses to consider
    • 2 Cor. 12: 9-10 (God’s strength seen in our weakness)
    • Mat 27: 46 (Jesus showing vulnerability on the cross)
    • 1 John 1:6-7 (Walking in the light)
(2 Cor. 12: 9-10) If we’re going to lead our mentee through difficult things, we must be transparent with our failures, our lessons learned, and what we still struggle with as we continue to learn. 

Not everyone’s learning process is going to be the same, but everyone of us has to learn how to rely on God through a process, it doesn’t just happen all at once and automatically (Philippians 4:11), so your mentee will benefit greatly to learn from your example. 

We should imitate Paul in this kind of transparency, in the same way that’s described in 2 Cor. 12:9-10. You shouldn’t be telling them to just be strong just like you. You should show them how God’s faithfulness during your own weakness made you stronger over time. 

There are risks associated with transparency. It’s possible the mentee will judge you, misunderstand you, slander you, or do other bad things. Please understand the mentee is taking those same risks with you. That trust must go both ways for the mentorship to work. 

Transparency is what allows you to be known. Knowing, but refusing to be known is a sign of failure in a mentor, so please understand you will fail if you refuse to be known. You can’t have a relationship when one or both people don’t know who the other person is. The substance of discipleship is relationship, so let yourself be known! Here are some practical tips.
    • Ask how much detail and what subjects the mentee can handle hearing about.
    • Be specific (as appropriate) about how God helps you in relevant areas of your life. 
    • Don’t hide things to preserve your reputation, self-image, or comfort zone. This is a huge part of the sacrifice we make as we show compassion and stay with them in their pain. 

(Mat 27: 46) Jesus shows many good examples of transparency. One of the most powerful is when he says “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”, while still on the cross. If there was ever as time to keep a brave face this would be it, but he shows us his vulnerability instead.

In doing this, he shows us what this kind of transparency should like like. It’s raw, has the potential to be tremendously embarrassing, and yet the Holy Spirit insisted on including this in the scripture for good reason. 
It shows God’s response to our pain isn’t made out of shallow platitudes like “just believe”, “don’t give up”, or “have mental grit”. While there is truth in them, God does so much more than this. On the cross he leads us through our pain in part by showing us his. 

As he shows us his pain, he points far more to God as the deliverer rather than the human response to suffering. We’re shown that God is with us, even in our despair. This is what helps, not some cheap response to our mentee, who paid a great cost in showing us courage though their vulnerability. So how should we respond?
    • Talk about how faith is a gift (Eph. 2: 8-9), which needs to be sought out. (Phil. 2: 12-13). God is the one who initiates, we have to respond to him with vulnerability.

    • Point out even severe and extended trials are a normal stage of spiritual development. They are not beyond God’s knowledge or reach. (Psalm 139: 7-12).

    • Acknowledge your experiences with doubt, disbelief, despair etc. and God’s role in moving you into a better place. Focus on how God’s actions led to your own, not the other way around. (2 Cor. 1: 8-10).

    • Remind the mentee that God can help them with their unbelief. (Mark 9:24).
(1 John 1:6-7) As we show transparency in the mentorship process, we shed light on one of the proofs that we have real relationship with Jesus. In fact, there is a direct relationship between our willingness to be known, which is to to walk in the light, and our maturity in Christ. 
Why? Because it shows our experience with being known and loved at the same time. This is what we want our mentees to experience too! 
    • Your confidence that you are known and still loved can be contagious. 
    • Walking in the light shows power over shame, the greatest enemy of transparency. 
    • Walking in the light shows power over other fears that cause people to hide. 
Part 3: Compassion
Verses to consider
    • Word study: Compassion, what does it mean?
    • Habakkuk 3:2 (Even in wrath, remember mercy).
    • John 16: 15-18 / John 15:26 (The comfort of the holy spirit)
(Word Study) The word compassion means “to suffer with”. This is more than empathy, which is only feeling the other person’s pain. Compassion means also entering that pain in a way that involves your presence, action, and sacrifice in their life. 
I’m going to be blunt about this, without compassion, all the wisdom in the world isn’t going to help your mentee. Your compassion and ability to communicate it will form a large part of the substance of your relationship with your mentee. Without that substance, there’s a good chance your efforts will be harmful, not helpful, even if your 100% right about the things you say. 
    • You can’t enter their pain without feeling it. Involvement of the heart is not optional.  
    • Compassion is first focused on providing relief, correction matters, but it comes later.
    • Compassion is pro-active and reactive. It seeks to relieve and prevent suffering.
(Habakkuk 3) In this chapter, we see a prayer to God even when the prophet knows that judgment is coming to Jerusalem. Although God’s people are about to suffer as the direct result of their own sin, Habakkuk still cries out to God to show them as much mercy as possible. What does this show us about the nature of God’s compassion?
    • He will not fully abandon his people, even as he disciplines them harshly.
    • He is with us and helps us overcome the consequences of our own sin.
    • If God shows compassion even in his wrath, how more should we show compassion when we preach God’s mercy in Jesus Christ? 
(John 16: 15-18 / John 15:26) Even though your compassion is needed, you’ll find that your supply is limited. Depending on the situation, the mentee may drain you much faster than expected, or difficulties in your own life may drain you as well. 
The good news is that Jesus never meant for your compassion to be the only place where your mentee gets it from! He gives us the holy spirit to rely on, often for things that other people simply can’t do. 
    • The Greek word Paraklētos is used to describe the Holy Spirit. This word means helper, comforter, counselor, and advocate all in one. 
    • The Holy Spirit lives inside your mentee, knowing their needs and what helps them.
    • Not everyone will feel the same things, but teaching the mentee to pursue the Holy Spirit will help them experience God’s comfort, not if, but when your comfort fails them.
Part 4: Surrender
Verses to consider
    • Proverbs 16:9 / James 4: 13-15 (We make our plans, but God leads us)
    • 1 Cor. 3:7 (Man plants / waters, but God makes us grow)
    • Matt. 10:14 (Sometimes people will reject good counsel)
(Proverbs 16:9 / James 4: 13-16) It’s all well and good for us to make a plan of action to help our mentee recover from their trial, but the reality is that God is healing our mentee on his timetable, not ours. Here are some things to keep in mind. 
    • They can’t just flip a switch and change their hearts, otherwise they wouldn’t need Jesus.
    • Sometimes people overcome things quickly, other times it takes decades, for others they struggle the rest of their lives. You don’t actually know how long it will take. 

(1 Cor. 3:7) Not only do we not know how fast our mentee will recover, we don’t have control over it either! With that said, it’s important for us to know what we do have control over. 

In 1 Cor. 3:7 we’re spoken of as if we are farmers planting seeds and watering them, but God is the one who causes the plants to grow. For our efforts here and now, our responsibility is to plant wisdom and nurture our mentee to the best of our ability, but it is not our responsibility to change them. 
    • Know the difference between planting a seed and forcing an idea on someone. 
    • Nurturing, not nagging your mentee gives that seed the best chance it has of growing. 
    • Growth may be visible or not. Your responsibility is to tend to the field regardless. 
(Matt. 10:14) As we invest time, energy, and hope into our mentees, we must deal with the possibility that they aren’t ready to make the changes that will help make things better. Even if we do everything right, the seeds may not grow, and it might turn out that our presence in their lives isn’t making the difference we hoped for. 
If we have tried all we know and shared all we can share and the mentee still won’t receive us, we must consider withdrawing ourselves from the mentor relationship. 
    • When spreading the Gospel, Jesus instructed the disciples to leave the towns they were not received in. He did not tell them to stay and force the issue.
    • We need to recognize if or when our mentee is not willing to receive us. This may require one or more clarifying conversations.

Wrapping Up

More than anything, our job as mentors is to show the character, compassion and wisdom of Christ as we work to help people through their difficult times. If we lack the humility, transparency, compassion, and willingness to surrender ourselves to Christ in this process, at some point the difficulty involved will lead us to cause more harm than good. 

There’s more to the character of Christ than merely these things, but if you’ve developed all of these characteristics in your life, you have a huge head start in showing your mentee what it looks like to be loved by Jesus. 

Please take an honest look at yourself to see if you’ve grown into the kind of person we need you to be to serve on this team. We hope that you’re ready to go and make a difference in the lives of the most broken among us.  

Addition 1: Boundaries

Truth is often found in tension. One of the most important truths we’ll discover as we mentor others is there will often be a tension between their needs and our own. There will also be a tension between our influence in their life and their own responsibilities. If we’re successful in managing those tensions, there’s a much better chance we can build a successful mentorship with them.

Verses to consider
    • John 15: 9-13 (Loving others from the love we receive from God.)
    • 1 Peter 4:15 (Don’t meddle or try and control what doesn’t belong to you)
    • Luke 6: 43-44 (You shall know a tree by its fruit)

(John 15: 9-13) One of the temptations when providing mentorship or any other service is going to be overextending ourselves. With our focus on Christ-like selfless love, it’s easy to feel guilty, or like we’ve failed if we find ourselves burnt out. But if we ignore our need for him, we teach them to ignore him as well as we set a bad example.

    • Jesus himself did not serve on this earth without receiving love from God the father.
    • Serving is not a heartless act of duty, but an overflow of the love of God in our hearts.
    • Ignoring our need for him leads us to serve out of the vanity of our own will.

(1 Peter 4:5) Another common boundary issue is the problem of meddling. That is, the idea of trying to get involved with, or to control things that you have no right to control. Meddling is such a severe issue, it’s listed right next to theft and murder as things we shouldn’t find ourselves guilty of. 

This is why having a heart surrendered to God that allows us to be aware of our own limits is such a big deal.  If we can’t see, or don’t care about where the line is between us and others, we will inevitably try and take control of other people’s choices in ways that make us more of a menace than a mentor. 

    • You are responsible for guiding your mentee, not making their choices.

    • Communicate clearly with your mentee about what healthy influence looks like. Make sure you don’t take an overbearing, agenda-driven approach. 

    • Indirect manipulation techniques are just as bad as overbearing ones. Being sneaky doesn’t make you less controlling, it just makes you more dishonest. 

(Luke 6:43-44) Sometimes it can be hard to know exactly how much involvement we should have with someone. What makes things even more complicated, is that our involvement may need to increase or decrease over time, even if we don’t see the need to change immediately. 

One of the best ways to deal with this problem is to regularly look at our relationship with the mentee in a way that shows us how their relationship with us affects both of our relationships with God. 
If we find that the fruit of the mentor relationship is seriously harming either of our relationships with God, it’s not bearing good fruit! at some point we’ll need to have less involvement, or withdraw entirely from the mentorship. 

Here are some thoughts to keep in mind:

    • You can only minister from the condition you are in. Allowing your relationship with God to dry out counts as bad fruit. This is a serious warning sign, look for it!

    • Doing things for God instead of doing things with God turns into idolatry and you can’t serve God by disobeying him. Again this is the kind of bad fruit to be conscious of.

    • Even with our best efforts, it’s possible the relationship still won’t bear good fruit. In such cases, it’s better to bow out gracefully than try and force things in our own strength.

Final Thoughts:
There is a line between where we end and God begins. The same is true between our mentee and God, as well as our mentee and ourselves. If we’re conscious of those lines, we can be aware of how much influence that we and our mentees have over each other and see if it’s healthy or not. 
We can see how the mentorship is affecting both of our relationships with God, as well as how it’s affecting the relationship between us and them. If we find over time that the mentorship isn’t bearing good fruit, and especially if it’s harming our relationship with God, it’s time to bow out.
My hope is that we’ll start off each mentorship in a way that is as close to healthy as we can possibly get, but realistically speaking, there’s a good chance we’ll need to adjust along the way. Boundaries can change over time as people and circumstances change, so be alert and responsive.
